GEOLOGY · BEGINNERS · ROCK IDENTIFICATION

Identifying River Rocks by Color, Pattern, and Density

By Paul Shoemaker · Published October 17, 2026

A riverbed can hold pink speckled stones, dark smooth cobbles, white quartz, and rocks crossed by pale ribbons. Learning to recognize them makes a day beside the water more interesting—and helps a prospector understand the materials moving through a watershed.

Begin with texture and pattern, then consider color and density. No single clue identifies every stone. A useful first identification might be “probably granite” or “a quartz-rich rock,” with a closer examination still to come.

The photographs below show identified examples, not every possible appearance. Each caption distinguishes a reference specimen from a photographed exposure or transported stone. Tap a photograph to enlarge it; use Close, Escape, or tap the enlarged photograph to return.

How rocks become river stones

“River rock” describes where a stone is found, not how it originally formed. A rounded cobble might once have belonged to a lava flow, a mountain’s granite core, or a bed of sandstone.

During transport, collisions and abrasion wear down edges. Experimental research by Domokos and colleagues on how river rocks become rounded shows that sharp corners can disappear before a stone’s overall dimensions shrink substantially. Roundness therefore does not provide a simple mileage counter.

A stone may also have traveled before entering its present river. Glaciers can carry rocks far from their original bedrock, leaving material that later becomes available for streams to move. The Missouri Geological Survey’s quartzite and glacial erratics guide gives examples of this long-distance transport. A loose cobble is a clue to a region’s history, not proof that identical bedrock lies immediately beneath it.

Three ways rocks form

Igneous rocks form when molten material cools and solidifies. Intrusive rocks cool underground; slower cooling commonly allows visible crystals to grow. Extrusive rocks form from material erupted at the surface, where faster cooling often produces much smaller crystals.

Sedimentary rocks form from accumulated sediment or material deposited from water. Sand grains can become sandstone; shell material can contribute to limestone.

Metamorphic rocks develop when existing rocks change under heat, pressure, and sometimes fluid activity without completely melting. Minerals may recrystallize, align, or form new combinations.

The British Geological Survey’s rocks and minerals introduction connects these three families to the rock cycle. “Intrusive” describes a rock’s formation; density describes its mass for a given volume. They are different properties.

Recognizing common stones

These descriptions are starting points. The mix of rocks in a particular river depends on its watershed and transport history. Separate photographs show separate examples; they are not before-and-after views of the same stone.

Granite

Granite often has an irregular mosaic of visible crystals. Look for pale feldspar, glassy gray quartz, and dark mineral flecks. Some examples are pink; others are mostly gray or white. Its crystals grew as magma cooled underground.

Diorite

Diorite can have a more evenly mixed black-and-white appearance, with abundant pale feldspar and dark minerals. It also forms underground. A speckled cobble should not automatically be called granite: mineral composition matters as well as appearance.

The National Park Service’s igneous rock guide compares these intrusive rocks and their minerals.

Basalt

Basalt is commonly dark gray or black, with crystals too small to distinguish easily by eye. It forms from cooling lava. Some pieces contain holes left by gas bubbles; others are compact and apparently uniform.

A dark, smooth cobble is only a basalt candidate. Weathering and river abrasion can hide identifying details, and other fine-grained rocks can look similar. Compare it with the basalt examples in the NPS igneous rock guide.

Sandstone

Sandstone contains cemented sand grains. A hand lens may reveal individual grains and changes in grain size between layers. Colors range widely; reddish sandstone often owes its color to iron oxides rather than to a fundamentally different rock family.

Limestone

Limestone is dominated by carbonate minerals, commonly calcite. Some pieces show shell fragments or other fossils; others look relatively uniform. Limestone can form through biological accumulation or chemical deposition, so not every specimen contains recognizable shells.

The NPS sedimentary rock guide explains how loose material becomes rock and illustrates several sedimentary textures.

Gneiss

Gneiss, pronounced “nice,” commonly shows contrasting mineral bands. Pale and dark zones may be straight, curved, or folded. This pattern developed during metamorphism and deformation; it is not necessarily a stack of original sediment layers.

Mica schist

Mica schist often has a glittering sheen from visible mica flakes arranged along a preferred direction. Look for the organization of those flakes across the stone, rather than one isolated sparkle.

The National Park Service’s Curecanti rock guide includes a photographed gneiss specimen and descriptions of both rocks. These are useful comparisons when a cobble looks striped or unusually reflective.

Quartzite

Quartzite develops when quartz-rich sandstone undergoes metamorphism. Its grains become tightly interlocked. Colors can include white, gray, pink, and red; some specimens preserve banding. The Missouri Geological Survey’s quartzite guide includes a specimen photograph and examples of colorful transported stones.

Marble

Marble forms when limestone or other carbonate-rich rock recrystallizes during metamorphism. Its crystalline texture can look sugary, and impurities may produce streaks or patches of color.

Both are commonly described as nonfoliated metamorphic rocks: they need not have the strongly aligned mineral fabric seen in schist. Compare the NPS metamorphic rock guide. A pale crystalline appearance alone will not reliably separate marble from quartzite.

Quartz

A solid white or translucent pebble may be mostly quartz, a mineral rather than a rock family. Quartz also occurs within granite, sandstone, quartzite, and many other rocks.

It has a Mohs hardness of 7, meaning it can scratch ordinary glass. That test identifies a property, not a unique rock name: several quartz-rich materials can do the same thing. See the Missouri Geological Survey’s quartz guide.

Chert

Chert consists largely of extremely fine crystalline silica. It can look uniform or mottled and commonly breaks along curved, shell-like surfaces. Colors include pale gray, brown, red, and nearly black. Jasper and flint are names applied to particular varieties.

Its resistance to weathering helps explain its abundance in some river gravels, as described in Missouri’s chert guide.

What colors and patterns can reveal

Pink crystals in granite may be feldspar. Rusty reds and yellows often involve iron-bearing minerals. Green can come from minerals such as chlorite and epidote. The USGS explains these relationships in what makes rocks colorful.

Greenstone

One example is greenstone: altered or metamorphosed basalt and related rocks can acquire green minerals. At Shenandoah, ancient basalt became greenstone as its minerals changed during mountain building. The park’s greenstone guide shows why the weathered outside and a fresher surface may look quite different.

Patterns deserve their own examination:

Patterns are clues to investigate, not a final identification
What you noticeWhat to investigate
Separate, interlocking crystalsAn igneous or recrystallized metamorphic texture
Distinct sand grainsSandstone or a related sedimentary rock
Alternating mineral bandsGneiss or another banded rock
Aligned shiny flakesMica-rich schist or another foliated rock
A narrow pale line cutting across other featuresA mineral vein or other later filling
Very fine texture with curved broken surfacesChert or another silica-rich material

A pale vein might contain quartz or carbonate minerals. Identifying the vein and identifying the surrounding rock are separate tasks. Geological descriptions such as Dennis P. Cox’s USGS polymetallic vein model illustrate how several minerals can occupy the same vein system. A white stripe alone does not establish gold content.

Comparing density

Density means mass divided by volume. Compare stones of the same volume: a larger piece of a less-dense rock can outweigh a smaller piece of a denser one. Density also differs from hardness, which measures resistance to scratching.

The following approximate rock ranges come from Penn State’s rock-density table. They are comparison values, not identification boundaries. Mineral proportions, pore space, weathering, and moisture can change a specimen’s measured density.

Approximate densities · grams per cubic centimeter (g/cm³)
MaterialApproximate density in g/cm³
Sandstone2.2–2.8
Limestone2.3–2.7
Marble2.4–2.7
Mica schist2.5–2.9
Granite2.6–2.7
Gneiss2.6–2.9
Quartzite2.6–2.8
Basalt2.8–3.0
Diorite2.8–3.0
Quartz mineralAbout 2.65
Pure goldAbout 19.3

Quartz and gold are mineral reference values, supported by the Open University’s explanation of density. Specific gravity compares density with water and is numerically close to density in g/cm³ under ordinary conditions.

For an illustrative comparison, equal 100 cm³ volumes would weigh about 265 grams for quartz and 1,930 grams for pure gold. Dividing 19.3 by 2.65 gives about 7.3: pure gold is roughly seven times as dense as quartz. Natural gold commonly contains other metals, so an actual specimen may be less dense.

Notice the overlap among ordinary rocks. Density might support an identification, but it cannot reliably distinguish granite, quartzite, marble, and gneiss by itself.

A simple way to examine a stone

  1. Observe it dry, then wet a small area. Record both appearances; wetting can make patterns easier to see.
  2. Use a hand lens. Look for grains, crystals, flakes, pores, fossils, and bands.
  3. Describe it before naming it. “Gray, fine-grained, with a pale crosscutting vein” is a useful observation even when the rock name is uncertain.
  4. Photograph it with a scale. Include several sides and note the location and whether it came from loose gravel or exposed bedrock.
  5. Compare more than one property. A plausible identification should fit the texture, composition, and local geology together.

For an accompanying lesson, geologist and educator Nick Zentner’s Rock Identification podcast episode presents an introductory identification lab.

At home, a compact, nonporous specimen can provide a simple density experiment: weigh it in grams, measure the milliliters of water it displaces, and divide mass by displaced volume. One milliliter equals one cubic centimeter. A 270-gram stone displacing 100 milliliters has an estimated density of 2.7 g/cm³. Trapped bubbles, water absorption, and imprecise volume readings can distort the result.

What this tells a gold prospector

The large density difference between gold and ordinary rock is part of what makes gravity concentration possible. The Wyoming State Geological Survey’s gold overview connects that difference with placer deposits.

Rock identification adds geological context, but a heavy stone, a quartz vein, or a rusty coating does not establish that gold is present. Use those observations alongside documented local geology and comparable test pans. Where stones have traveled far, be especially cautious about assuming that a loose cobble points directly to nearby bedrock.

Start with three stones on your next visit: one speckled, one banded, and one apparently uniform. Describe their differences before reaching for names. That small habit turns a riverbed full of anonymous rocks into evidence you can compare from trip to trip.
